Consultation, seen 06/16/2020

documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
KESTREL HILL NEUROLOGY, Neuromuscular Clinic
New patient consultation, 06/08/2021

Patient: Tyler Boucher, 29-year-old man
Referred by: PCP

Reason for referral: Several years of increasing difficulty keeping pace with coworkers at physical labor, with limb weakness and episodes of double vision.

History: Mr. Boucher says that as a boy he could take part in most sports but always ran out of energy ahead of the other kids. Over the last year the weakness in his arms and legs has come on more often, chiefly after he climbs several flights of stairs. He also has spells of diplopia and trouble keeping his eyes focused for long stretches. He has never had a head injury, a seizure or a faint. He works in construction and reports no toxic or solvent exposures.

Past medical history: seasonal allergic rhinitis on subcutaneous immunotherapy; lifelong exercise intolerance. Tonsillectomy age 12.
Medications: cetirizine 10 mg daily as needed, fluticasone nasal spray daily, allergen immunotherapy injections monthly.
Allergies: tree, grass and weed pollen. No drug allergies.
Family history: mother developed a similar picture in her 30s. Several maternal relatives with hearing loss beginning early in life.
Social: construction work. Never smoker. Alcohol 1-2 drinks weekly.

Examination:
General: thin young man, in no distress.
Cardiac: regular rate and rhythm, no murmur. Lungs: clear.
Cranial nerves: bilateral ptosis. Extraocular movements limited in more than one direction of gaze. Pupils equal and reactive. Facial strength and bulbar function normal. Hearing grossly intact to conversation.
Motor: normal bulk and tone. Mild weakness of the proximal limb muscles, upper and lower, symmetric. Distal strength full.
Reflexes: 2+ throughout, toes downgoing.
Sensory: intact to all modalities.
Coordination and gait: normal.

Impression: Slowly progressive proximal myopathy with ptosis and ophthalmoparesis and a lifelong history of early fatigue, with a similar history in his mother and early hearing loss on the maternal side. The picture raises concern for a mitochondrial myopathy.

Plan:
1. Creatine kinase, TSH, resting lactate on two occasions, and lactate after a brief standardized exertion.
2. EMG/nerve conduction studies.
3. Muscle biopsy with histochemistry.
We will write again once results are available.

Neurology, Kestrel Hill Neurology
cc: PCP

reports.text:
Kestrel Hill Neurology EMG Laboratory. Indication: proximal weakness, ptosis.
Nerve conduction studies: median, ulnar and peroneal motor and median, ulnar and sural sensory responses have normal latencies, amplitudes and conduction velocities bilaterally where tested. F-waves normal.
Repetitive nerve stimulation not performed.
Needle EMG: deltoid, biceps, iliopsoas and vastus lateralis bilaterally show short-duration, low-amplitude, polyphasic motor unit potentials with early recruitment. No fibrillations or positive sharp waves. Distal muscles (first dorsal interosseous, tibialis anterior) normal.
reports.conclusion: Myopathic pattern in proximal muscles. No evidence of neuropathy.

reports.text:
Specimen: skeletal muscle, left vastus lateralis, open biopsy.
Frozen sections with routine and enzyme histochemistry.
Microscopic: fibers of irregular, uneven shape with mild variation in fiber size. Modified Gomori trichrome stain shows collections of abnormal mitochondria accumulated beneath the sarcolemma in scattered fibers. No inflammatory infiltrate. No necrosis. No vacuoles.
reports.conclusion: Skeletal muscle with subsarcolemmal accumulation of abnormal mitochondria on modified Gomori trichrome, consistent with a mitochondrial myopathy.

KESTREL HILL NEUROLOGY, Neuromuscular Clinic
Results letter, 07/20/2021

Re: Tyler Boucher, DOB 07/29/1991

Dear Doctor,

I have now reviewed the full workup on Mr. Boucher, whom I saw on 06/08 for proximal weakness, ptosis and diplopia, and went over it with him by phone today.

Laboratory:
- Creatine kinase 612 U/L (elevated).
- Lactate at rest 3.4 mmol/L (06/08) and 3.1 mmol/L (06/22), both high; 5.8 mmol/L after minimal exertion on 06/22, higher still.
- TSH 1.8 mIU/L, normal.

EMG/NCS (06/29): myopathic motor units in proximal muscles; nerve conduction normal.

Muscle biopsy, left vastus lateralis (07/06): irregularly shaped fibers, with abnormal mitochondria collected under the fiber membrane on modified Gomori trichrome stain.

Diagnosis: Mitochondrial myopathy. The persistently raised resting lactate that climbs further with exertion, the myopathic EMG and the biopsy findings fit together, and his mother's history supports a familial disorder. His lifelong exercise intolerance is part of the same condition.

Plan: There is no disease-specific medication for this condition, and I am not starting a supplement. Because mitochondrial disease can involve the heart and hearing, and given the early hearing loss on his mother's side, I have arranged a baseline ECG and hearing test, and I will see him on 08/17 to go over them and set up a graded exercise program. After that I will review him yearly.

I discussed the diagnosis with him and answered his questions. Reports enclosed.

Sincerely,
Neurology, Kestrel Hill Neurology

HPI: Mr. Boucher has had worsening shortness of breath for about 18 months and is now breathless with very little effort. He used to jog regularly at an easy pace; now two blocks of walking leave him winded. He occasionally feels a mild tightness in the chest. He denies chest pain, wheezing, cough or hemoptysis. He has never smoked.

Meds: cetirizine 10 mg PRN, fluticasone nasal 2 sprays each nostril daily, monthly allergen immunotherapy.
Allergies: tree, grass and weed pollen; no drug allergies.
Family history: father died in his mid-40s of cirrhosis that was attributed to alcohol; the patient recalls his father having chronic breathing problems. Paternal grandmother with cirrhosis of unknown cause.
Social: freelance graphic designer, works from home. Never smoker. Drinks socially. No recreational drugs. No pets.

Exam:
Vital signs normal other than respiratory rate 22 and SpO2 94% on room air.
General: thin, mildly tachypneic at rest, no accessory muscle use.
Lungs: no crackles or wheeze; expiratory phase mildly prolonged; hyperresonant to percussion bilaterally.
Cardiac: regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, no murmur.
Extremities: no clubbing, no cyanosis, no edema.

- Labs today: ALT 64 U/L and AST 52 U/L, both mildly elevated. Remainder of hepatic panel normal.

Re: Tyler Boucher, DOB 07/29/1991

Further to my consultation of 06/13:

Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin: 28 mg/dL (low).
Phenotype: PiZZ.

Diagnosis: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, ZZ phenotype. The lower-lobe emphysema pattern on his chest x-ray and the airflow obstruction with air trapping on PFTs represent the lung disease of his alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. His mildly raised transaminases on 06/13 (ALT 64, AST 52) are noted.

3. I will see him yearly with spirometry, sooner if his breathing changes.

I called Tyler today with the results and the plan and answered his questions. In light of this result he wondered whether his father's illness was the same condition.

Sincerely,
Pulmonology, Sugarloaf Pulmonary Associates

WESTMERE REGIONAL HOSPITAL, BEHAVIORAL HEALTH UNIT
Psychiatric Admission Evaluation
Date of admission: 06/09/2026

Patient: Tyler Boucher, 34-year-old man

Reason for admission: inpatient stabilization of psychotic symptoms.

History of present illness: Over roughly the past 8 months Mr. Boucher has been hearing voices that others do not hear. His speech has become increasingly disorganized and difficult to follow, and he has withdrawn from the people around him. No prior psychiatric treatment or hospitalization.

Psychiatric history: none prior.
Medical history: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ) with emphysema; mitochondrial myopathy; seasonal allergic rhinitis on subcutaneous immunotherapy; exercise intolerance.
Surgical: tonsillectomy.
Home medications: cetirizine 10 mg daily as needed; fluticasone propionate nasal spray 2 sprays per nostril daily; monthly allergen immunotherapy (outside); albuterol HFA 2 puffs every 4 to 6 hours as needed; alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor (human) 60 mg/kg IV weekly by home infusion (pulmonology).
Allergies: tree, grass and weed pollen. No known drug allergies.
Family history: maternal uncle with schizophrenia. Identical twin brother, well, with no psychiatric illness; he has been in touch with the team and has asked about his own chances of developing a similar illness. Mother has mitochondrial myopathy. Father, now deceased, had alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
Social history: freelance graphic designer. Never smoker. Alcohol socially, 1-2 drinks per week. Denies recreational drug use.

Mental status examination: Alert and cooperative. Speech disorganized and at times hard to follow. Reports auditory hallucinations. Socially withdrawn on the unit. Denies suicidal or homicidal ideation. Oriented to person, place and time.

Assessment: Symptoms meet DSM-5 criteria for schizophrenia.

Plan:
1. Admit to the behavioral health unit for stabilization.
2. Start risperidone 2 mg by mouth daily.
3. Start benztropine 1 mg by mouth twice daily.
4. Continue cetirizine, fluticasone and albuterol as needed. Hold the weekly augmentation infusions during the admission; resume at home after discharge.
5. Social work and family meeting; team to meet with his brother regarding his question.

Attending Psychiatrist, Behavioral Health Unit

documents.body:
WESTMERE REGIONAL HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Provider note, arrival 07/03/2026 14:25 (Friday)

CC: confusion

HPI: 34-year-old man, discharged from our behavioral health unit one week ago with a new diagnosis of schizophrenia, started there on risperidone 2 mg daily and benztropine 1 mg twice daily. Also has alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and mitochondrial myopathy. For the last two days he has been confused and restless, eating and drinking very little, and complains his vision is blurry. His roommate, who brought him, says he has been behaving strangely, talking to himself, and will not eat or drink. The patient says he feels much too hot. History limited by his mental status; obtained from roommate and our discharge records.

Meds (per discharge list): risperidone 2 mg daily; benztropine 1 mg BID; cetirizine 10 mg PRN; fluticasone nasal; monthly allergen immunotherapy; albuterol PRN; alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor IV weekly by home infusion.
Allergies on arrival: tree/grass/weed pollen; no drug allergies.
PMH: schizophrenia (06/2026), AATD (PiZZ) with emphysema, mitochondrial myopathy, allergic rhinitis.

Exam:
T 38.1 C (100.6 F), HR 104, BP 152/88, RR 18, SpO2 95% RA.
General: restless, not in respiratory distress.
Skin: flushed, warm and dry. No rash.
HEENT: mucous membranes dry. Pupils 5 mm bilaterally, sluggishly reactive to light.
Neck: supple.
CV: tachycardic, regular, no murmur.
Lungs: clear, no crackles.
Abdomen: soft, nontender, bladder not palpable.
Neuro: no rigidity, no clonus, no tremor. Moves all extremities. Inattentive; disoriented to time and place.

Workup:
- CBC: within normal limits.
- BMP: within normal limits.
- CK 549 U/L; near his chronic baseline in the 500s with known mitochondrial myopathy.
- Urinalysis: unremarkable.

MDM: Delirium with fever, tachycardia, hypertension, flushed dry skin, dry mucosa, mydriasis and blurred vision, one week after starting benztropine: anticholinergic toxicity from benztropine. No rigidity and CK at his baseline make neuroleptic malignant syndrome unlikely. Labs otherwise reassuring.

ED course: benztropine held. IV normal saline. Cooling measures and a low-stimulation room. Placed in observation for serial reassessment.

Diagnosis: Adverse effect of anticholinergic medication (benztropine) with delirium.
Benztropine discontinued. Benztropine (anticholinergic toxicity) entered as a drug allergy.

Emergency Medicine Attending
